A new believer needs to know that the gap between being declared right with God and feeling fully changed isn't a defect in his experience. It's the normal shape of the Christian life. The tradition has carefully distinguished justification, the once-for-all declaration that a person stands accepted by God on the basis of Christ's work and not his own, from sanctification, the slow work of the Spirit making that person like Christ over a lifetime. It has insisted that the first grounds the second: we're changed because we're accepted, never accepted because we're changed.

That guards against two cliffs. On one side is the moralism that turns acceptance into performance and leaves a believer forever anxious about whether he has done enough. On the other is the error that seizes on free grace and concludes that since acceptance is unearned, growth is optional and sin no longer matters, which the New Testament flatly rejects. Set this beside our impatience for instant change, the expectation that real transformation should be fast and visible and complete, and ask what that does to someone being changed at the pace of an actual human life. Talk about how to hold assurance and effort together: resting fully in an acceptance already secured while really pressing on in obedience, neither earning what is given nor neglecting what is meant to grow. And recover some of the patience older Christians had with their own slow progress, walking a long road with a Christ who declares them righteous now and is patiently making them so.

memoryVerse.text: And he said to all, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me."

leaderPrimer:
Leading this study is closer to holding a newborn than to teaching a class, and the first mistake is the one that comes most naturally to people who have believed a long time. We bury the beginning in vocabulary. Justification, sanctification, quiet time, walking with the Lord: all the shorthand that took us years to stop noticing lands on a two-week-old faith like a load on a seedling, and the new believer concludes that everyone else got a manual and he missed the day it was handed out. Watch your language. Explain each church word in plain English the first time it comes up.

Watch the level of the room too. A well-meaning longtime Christian may wander in wanting to raise controversies and correct wording. His knowledge may be real, but his timing is wrong. Keep the room at the level of first steps, kindly and firmly.

The order you must guard above everything is the order of the gospel itself: love first, then everything else. The reading, the praying, the belonging and the turning all grow out of a love already given, and none of them earns or keeps that love. If this study becomes a checklist a beginner performs to feel acceptable, you'll have rebuilt the very religion the gospel came to end.

Then make the beginning normal, more often than feels necessary, because shame is loud. The high that faded was weather, not the thing itself. The sins they keep discovering mean they're awake, not failing. Nobody knows how to pray at first, including the twelve, which is why they asked.

There may well be a seeker at your table who doesn't yet believe and is watching to see what he'd be signing up for. Don't recruit him and don't single him out. Let him ask his hardest questions and find the questions welcome. When you pray to close each night, pray plainly, short and true and unembarrassed, because the group is learning what ordinary prayer sounds like from you.

The fifth session ends on a road, not an arrival. Send them out walking, unfinished, and not alone. That's the truest thing you can give them.

faq.q: Is this study going to make me perform or prove my faith before I'm ready?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to prevent exactly that. The whole study keeps to one order: the love came first, and the change grows out of it, never the other way round. Leaders are asked to say so out loud more than once. You aren't reading the Bible, praying, finding a church or turning from sin in order to earn God's love or keep it. The love was given before you cleaned up anything. The first session reassures you that the fading of the first feeling doesn't mean the thing wasn't real, and the last tells you plainly that still struggling with the same sins is a sign of life, not of fraud. If you came braced for a treadmill of religious performance, you'll find a study built to take the weight off.

faq.q: What if I don't feel anything anymore? The first weeks were powerful and now I feel nothing. Was it real?
faq.a: It almost certainly was, and the first session is built around exactly this fear. The feeling you had was real and good, but the new birth was never a feeling. It was something God did. Feelings are weather; they roll in and roll out while the fact of what happened holds. Scripture doesn't say you're saved as long as the glow lasts. It says you were born again, "not of perishable seed but of imperishable" (1 Peter 1:23), and a newborn doesn't stop being alive when the exciting morning of its birth is over. Some people feel fear rather than joy at the beginning, and they're as born again that frightened morning as they'll ever be. Your assurance rests on what God did, and God doesn't undo a birth because the baby is having a hard week.

faq.q: I tried to read the Bible and got completely lost. Am I just not smart enough or spiritual enough for it?
faq.a: No. You did what nearly every beginner does and started on page one, which strands most people in the ancient laws. The Bible isn't one book to read front to back. It's a library of sixty-six books written over many centuries, and the second session suggests starting somewhere else entirely: with Mark, the shortest account of Jesus' life, one chapter a day. The whole library has one person at its center, and you read to meet him first; after that the rest slowly makes sense. The first habit is the plainest one: ask what the passage says before you ask what it means for you. What you ran into was a method problem, not a soul problem.

faq.q: I don't know how to pray and I feel like I'm doing it wrong. What's the secret?
faq.a: There's no secret and no special language, and the third session exists to free you from the fear that there is. When Jesus' friends asked him to teach them to pray, he told them to begin with "Father," the plainest word a small child has. So the whole idea that you need to be fluent is false. Prayer is plain speech to a Father who already knows everything you're about to say and stays anyway. Short and true beats long and impressive, because God isn't grading the grammar. The disciples who walked with Jesus every day still had to ask him how, so not knowing is where everyone starts. And if you aren't sure anyone is listening, you may pray that too. Some of the most honest prayers in the Bible are people telling God they're not sure where he is.

faq.q: I love Jesus but I'm done with church. Why does this study say I can't follow alone?
faq.a: Because the New Testament can hardly imagine a Christian alone, and the fourth session takes your wound seriously while questioning the conclusion. If a church hurt you, that hurt is real, and the study doesn't wave it off or tell you to go back to the place that wounded you. But the "just me and Jesus" plan removes the very place faith is meant to grow, because nearly everything Christ commands, forgive one another, bear one another's burdens, love one another, can't be practiced alone. The church isn't a building or a brand you consume. The word means people, a family. You aren't looking for a perfect church, because there isn't one. You're looking for a place where the Bible is taken seriously and the people are truthful about needing grace.

faq.q: Does following Jesus eventually just turn into a list of rules I have to keep?
faq.a: No, and the fifth session names this fear and answers it with the order, which is everything. You don't obey to keep God happy with you. God was already for you; the love came first, before you changed a single thing, and nothing you do or stop doing earns it or loses it. Obedience isn't the rent you pay to stay loved. It's the way a life rearranges itself once a new center has moved in, the way anyone in love finds his whole life reorganizing around the person, not because a rulebook arrived but because a person did. Repentance isn't a one-time entry fee but a direction you keep turning. The change is real, and following does cost everything, but it's the cost of love reordering a life, not a treadmill of demands.

faq.q: I keep failing at the same things even after coming to Jesus. Does that mean I'm a fraud?
faq.a: No. It means you're on the road and not at the end of it, which is where every Christian who has ever lived has been. The fifth session is plain about this because this fear drives so many new believers back out the door. Repentance is a direction, a daily turning, not a one-time fee you paid and failed to honor, and having to turn from the same things again is the normal experience of being changed slowly over years rather than overnight. Believers decades in still repent of things they repented of at the beginning. The goal was never to be sinless by next week. It's a life pointed in a new direction, turning again whenever it drifts, carried by a Christ who knew exactly what he was getting when he took you and took you anyway.

faq.q: Can a seeker who isn't sure they believe yet come to this study?
faq.a: Yes, and the study is built with room for exactly that person. It takes doubt seriously rather than treating it as a problem to fix by the end of the night. Leaders are told not to pressure or single out the seeker, to let him ask his hardest questions, and to make the room a safe place to doubt. You're allowed to say "I'm not sure I believe this" and be met with welcome rather than anxious persuasion. The session on prayer tells you that you may pray your doubt out loud to God, and the session on the Bible invites you to keep your hard questions and write them down while you read. Some things are only learned from the inside, so a seeker is welcome to look from the inside while deciding.

faq.q: Do I need a dramatic testimony for my conversion to count?
faq.a: No, and the first session works to free you from that comparison. New believers measure themselves against dramatic stories they've heard and conclude their own quieter or stranger beginning doesn't count. But the new birth is something God did, not a feeling you produced or a cinematic moment you staged, and it doesn't need goosebumps or tears to be real. Many real beginnings, especially out of unbelief, are frightened rather than warm, full of grief for a certainty being lost, and they're as real a new birth as any. The study asks you to write the plainest account you can of what actually happened, in your own words, so you stop performing someone else's testimony and own yours. What makes it count isn't the drama. It's what God did.

faq.q: Why does the study assume nothing and explain every church word?
faq.a: Because the first steps aren't obvious, and pretending they are is one of the quickest ways to make a beginner feel he doesn't belong. Opening a Bible and understanding nothing, not knowing how to pray, being tempted to follow alone: these are ordinary parts of starting out, not signs of failure. So the study explains as it goes and asks every leader to speak as a fellow beginner, not an expert. You can't welcome someone into something while pretending you never had to find your own way into it. A leader who can say, "I'm still learning, still turning, still unsure about some things," can walk beside a new believer, and that's where real encouragement comes from.

faq.q: Does this study promise that following Jesus will be easy or make my problems go away?
faq.a: No, and it deliberately refuses to. It's open about the fact that following costs everything, that the road is long, that you'll keep failing and turning, that the church will sometimes hurt you, and that hard questions won't all be answered on schedule. The fifth session ends on purpose with a road stretching ahead rather than a finish line, because the Christian life doesn't get a tidy ending this side of heaven. What the study promises isn't an easy life or a quick arrival but a Companion for the long walk: a Christ who came first with love, who walks the road beside you, and who has promised to finish what he started.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm still pretty new myself, or still struggle with the basics?
faq.a: Being new doesn't disqualify you. It may be one of your best qualifications. The study is built to be led by a fellow beginner, not an expert who has it all worked out. Every discussion question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice, so you aren't improvising. Your openness about your own clumsy beginning, your unanswered questions and your ongoing turning from the same old things may be the most encouraging thing in the room. It gives others permission to stop performing a mastery no one actually has. What you do need is to get the order right and guard it, love before change, always; to treat the small, frightened beginning as normal so no one is ashamed of it; to keep the room safe for the wounded and welcoming for the doubter; and to point everyone, yourself first, toward the one who said, "follow me." Read the leader primer, remember your own beginning, and trust the material.

timeline.event: Jesus calls his first disciples with the words "follow me" (Mark 1:17), beginning discipleship as a walk behind a Person rather than the mastery of a system. The fifth session rests on this.

Jesus tells Nicodemus, who comes to him by night, that he must be born again, or born from above (John 3:3), naming the change at the center of the Christian life as a birth received rather than a self-improvement achieved. The ground of the first session.

The disciples, having watched Jesus pray, ask him to teach them how (Luke 11:1). He answers with a short, plain prayer that begins with "Father," setting prayer as a child's speech to a parent rather than a performance in a special language.

At Pentecost the first community forms and devotes itself "to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers" (Acts 2:42), sharing its life. From the start the faith is lived as a people, not alone.

Paul writes letters to young churches full of brand-new believers, addressing them not as finished saints but as people being slowly changed, and grounding every command in grace already given. This is the order the fifth session insists on.

First Peter tells believers they have been "born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable" (1 Peter 1:23) and are now "a chosen race, a royal priesthood" (1 Peter 2:9), naming both the new birth and the shared identity the first and fourth sessions explore.

Cyprian of Carthage, in On the Unity of the Church, argues that no one can have God for his Father who does not have the church for his mother, an early and strong statement that following was never meant to be solitary.

Augustine, who came to faith in his early thirties after years of searching, writes his Confessions, a candid account of a beginning and of the slow, lifelong reordering of a life around a new center.

The Reformers recover the conviction that a believer can know he belongs to Christ, resting assurance on God's finished work rather than on shifting feelings. This is the ground the first session offers the anxious new believer.

John Bunyan publishes The Pilgrim's Progress, picturing the Christian life as a long road walked with companions, through real danger, toward a city. It's the image behind the fifth session's road with no quick arrival.

C. S. Lewis, who came to faith as an adult after years of atheism, gives the wartime BBC talks later gathered as Mere Christianity (1952), a modern witness that one can come to faith from unbelief and learn the first steps late.

Eugene Peterson publishes A Long Obedience in the Same Direction, recovering for a hurried age the truth that discipleship is long, slow, ordinary faithfulness rather than a burst of intensity. It anchors the fifth session's long road.
Dane Ortlund publishes Gentle and Lowly, drawing attention to Christ's heart toward sinners and sufferers, the kindness the fifth session promises a new believer will find along the road.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. A special welcome to anyone for whom this is brand new, or anyone still deciding what they believe. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say "I don't understand" here. You can say "I'm not sure I believe this" here. Nobody will pressure you or quiz you or expect you to perform a faith you don't have. Second, everything we talk about runs on grace, the old word for love you didn't earn and can't pay back. You're not here to prove or earn anything. The love came first, and everything else grows out of it. Third, none of us is an expert teaching beginners. We're all beginners in some way, and I'll go first whenever it counts. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only true ones, and not knowing is a perfectly good place to start.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the week ahead, into real mornings and real decisions, because that's where first steps are either taken or not. Nobody here is expected to have arrived. We're just taking the next small step, together.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't all wrapped up, because following Jesus is a long road and not a quick arrival, and pretending otherwise wouldn't help you. Take one small step this week rather than trying to do everything at once. Try the practice, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. If you have a hard question that didn't get answered tonight, that's fine. Write it down and keep it, because some things are learned slowly, from the inside, as you walk. Let me pray for us before we go, plainly and briefly, the way we talked about. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this room, especially if all of this is new.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and grace, welcome any seekers plainly, and walk slowly through session 1's opening questions. Say out loud that a beginning is allowed to be small.
Week 2: Session 1, What Just Happened to Me, full discussion and practice on the new birth and assurance.
Week 3: Session 2, The Word, and How to Read It, with extra time on starting in Mark and the habit of asking what it says.
Week 4: Session 3, Prayer, Talking with the Father, part one: "Father" and freedom from special language.
Week 5: Session 3 continued: short and true prayer, praying the doubt, and time for anyone unsure whether anyone is listening.
Week 6: Session 4, The Church, You Cannot Follow Alone, taking wounds seriously and looking for an imperfect but faithful church.
Week 7: Session 5, Following, the Long Road: love before change, and repentance as a lifelong direction.

Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices and the Scripture index, and build the small practice card together, with room for anyone ready to take a next step such as baptism or joining a church.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together: what just happened, and how to read the Bible, starting in Mark.
Week 2: Session 3, Prayer, Talking with the Father, with extra time on praying plainly and praying the doubt.
Week 3: Session 4, The Church, You Cannot Follow Alone: the wound taken seriously, and the imperfect church.
Week 4: Session 5, Following, the Long Road, plus a short integration close and building the small practice card.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, What Just Happened to Me.
Week 2: Session 2, The Word, and How to Read It.
Week 3: Session 3, Prayer, Talking with the Father.
Week 4: Session 4, The Church, You Cannot Follow Alone.
Week 5: Session 5, Following, the Long Road.

bibliography.title: Mere Christianity
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The classic reasoned case for the faith (1952, from wartime radio talks) by a man who came to it from atheism. Warm and plain, useful for the seeker in the room and for the first session's treatment of conversion from unbelief.

bibliography.title: A Long Obedience in the Same Direction
bibliography.author: Eugene Peterson
bibliography.note: Peterson (1980) on discipleship as slow, ordinary, lifelong faithfulness rather than a burst of intensity. The pastoral backbone of session 5.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: Ortlund (2020) draws out the gentle and lowly heart of Christ toward the struggling, the kindness a new believer will find along the road. Sets the tone for session 5.

bibliography.title: Basic Christianity
bibliography.author: John Stott
bibliography.note: A clear, unhurried introduction (1958) to who Christ is and what it means to follow him, written for inquirers and new believers. Useful across all five sessions.

bibliography.title: The Pilgrim's Progress
bibliography.author: John Bunyan
bibliography.note: The enduring allegory (1678) of the Christian life as a long road walked with companions toward a city, the image behind session 5.

bibliography.title: Knowing God
bibliography.author: J. I. Packer
bibliography.note: Packer (1973) on the heart of the faith as knowing God personally rather than merely knowing about him. Supports session 2's aim of reading the Bible to meet a person.

bibliography.title: How to Read the Bible Book by Book
bibliography.author: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart
bibliography.note: A practical guide to reading each book of Scripture as the kind of writing it is. A good next step after session 2's start in Mark.

bibliography.title: The Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Augustine's account of his own beginning and the slow reordering of a life around a new center (about 400). Background for sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: Life Together
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Bonhoeffer on the gift and the reality of Christian community, refusing both the dream of a perfect fellowship and the isolation that starves faith. Background for session 4.

bibliography.title: Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Keller (2014) on prayer as relationship rather than technique. Useful for session 3.

bibliography.title: Celebration of Discipline
bibliography.author: Richard Foster
bibliography.note: Foster (1978) introduces the ordinary practices that sustain faith over years. Useful alongside session 5's small practice card.

bibliography.title: The Reason for God: Belief in an Age of Skepticism
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Keller (2008) takes the doubter's hard questions seriously rather than waving them off. Useful for the seeker in the room and for the questions raised in sessions 1 and 2.

glossary.definition: The old word for love you didn't earn and can't pay back. The whole Christian life begins and runs on it. You aren't loved because you changed; you change because you're loved, and getting that order right is the heart of this study.

Jesus' phrase to Nicodemus for what happens at conversion: being born again, or born from above (John 3:3). It names the change as something God does to a person rather than a self-improvement he achieves, which is why assurance rests on God's work and not on how we feel.

The settled knowledge that you belong to Christ, meant to be had rather than endlessly chased (1 John 5:13). It rests first on what God has done, not on the weather of your emotions, which rise and fall while the fact of the new birth holds.

The word means good news. It's news rather than advice: the announcement of what God has done in Christ for people who couldn't do it for themselves. Everything a new believer is asked to do is a response to this news, never a way of earning it.

The long, slow learning to live as a student of Jesus, walked over years rather than completed at the start. It's following a Person down a road, not mastering a system, which is why the beginning is allowed to be small.

The shortest of the four Gospels, the four accounts of Jesus' life, and the suggested place for a new believer to begin reading, one chapter at a time, to meet the person at the center of the whole Bible before taking on the rest of the library.

Plain speech to a Father who already knows everything you're about to say and stays anyway. It needs no special language and no minimum performance, since Jesus taught his friends to begin with the plainest word a child has, "Father."

Not a building or a brand but people: a body, a family of ordinary, imperfect believers you belong to. The New Testament word, ekklesia, meant an assembly or gathering, and the New Testament assumes that following Jesus is done with and for others, never alone.

Not groveling and not a one-time entry fee, but turning, changing direction. It's a daily, lifelong direction a believer keeps choosing whenever he drifts, so still having things to turn from is the normal experience of a living faith, not proof of fraud.

Not the rent paid to stay loved, but the shape a reordered life takes once a new center has moved in. Like the way any great love rearranges a life, it flows out of the love already given rather than working to earn it.

The church's word for the lifelong process by which a believer is actually changed and slowly made like Christ. It rests on an acceptance already secured, never the means of earning it, and it moves at the slow pace of a real human life.

The once-for-all declaration that a person stands accepted by God on the basis of Christ's work and not his own. It grounds all the change that follows, so a believer is changed because he's accepted, never accepted because he's changed.

The old word for telling God the truth when things hurt, unedited. Scripture is full of it, which is why a new believer may bring grief, anger and even doubt to God in prayer rather than editing them out.

Not a list of rules but a small set of chosen practices, like a trellis, that holds a life up so it can grow in one direction over years. A new believer can build one small enough to keep on his worst week, from the practices that actually helped.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Something real happened, and nobody handed you a manual. This five-session study, written for brand-new Christians and the recently baptized, walks slowly through the first steps of following Jesus: what just happened to you and how you can know it was real; how to read the Bible without getting lost on page one; how to pray when you don't know how; why you can't follow alone; and what the long road of following looks like over years. It runs on grace from start to finish, never loads a beginner with rules, and welcomes the seeker who's still deciding. Come new. Come unsure. Come as you are.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study called The First Steps, written for anyone who has recently come to faith, been baptized, or is simply wondering what following Jesus would mean. It's for beginners, and it treats beginners gently. It won't bury you in rules or expect you to have it all worked out. It covers what happened to you, how to read the Bible, how to pray, how to find your people, and the long road ahead, all in plain words, with every church term explained. Doubters are welcome too. No homework, and you don't need special preparation to lead a group. If you're new to all this, or thinking about it, this is for you. Sign up at the welcome table.

quoteCards: The new birth isn't finally a feeling. Feelings are weather. What God did doesn't evaporate when Tuesday is gray.
Don't start the Bible at page one. Start with Mark, and read to meet the person at the center.
When the disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray, he gave them one word to start with. Father.
Short and true beats long and impressive. God isn't grading the grammar.
You're not looking for a perfect church. If you found one, your joining would ruin it.
The "just me and Jesus" plan removes the very place faith was meant to grow.
You don't change in order to be loved. You change because you already are.
He isn't standing at the finish line judging your pace. He's on the road beside you, the whole way.
